scripts.opening:opening:
[warmly] Meet the Glessner House.

[short pause] A summer morning, 1904, at 1800 Prairie Avenue. The morning sun off the lake is on the granite front. Behind it live John J. Glessner, a farm-machinery man from Ohio... his wife Frances, who has kept a journal since 1879... [amused] and the house that shocked the street.

Ten stops on foot, all the way round one house: the corner, the Eighteenth Street side, the alley, the front door, the carriage passage, and the courtyard inside. The story is mostly the owner's own, from the account he wrote for his children in 1923. Exteriors only.

[short pause] [mischievously] Let's start at the corner, where the neighbors first saw it... and did not like what they saw.
scripts.stop:corner: [wistfully] An old Chicago saying called Prairie Avenue 'the sunny street that holds the sifted few'. Pullman's mansion stands diagonally across the corner, Kimball's French chateau across the avenue. [short pause] [amused] Then there is this one: rough granite, small deep windows, steep red roofs. It was the last house Henry Hobson Richardson designed... [softly] and he never saw it built.
scripts.stop:north-wall: [curious] This is the side people talked about when the house was new. Passers-by remarked on the narrow windows, 'just enough to light the narrow corridors'. [amused] Richardson held that the windows of a city house were 'not to look out of': people only shroud them in shades and curtains. [short pause] The house keeps its back to the street.
scripts.stop:arch: The great arch is the back door: a small corridor through it leads to the kitchen. [mischievously] It is also how the orchestra sneaks in. [whispers] On New Year's Day 1903 a double quartet of horns slipped in by the Eighteenth Street door and up the back stairs... [excited] and at four o'clock began to play in the upper hall.
scripts.stop:stable: The west wing is the stable and carriage house, with its wide carriage doorway onto Eighteenth Street. Inside, its walls are white glazed brick. [short pause] The furnace room is underneath it, so the dust, dirt and noise of coal and ashes never come into the house itself.
scripts.stop:gate: Round the corner, these gates in the alley open into the courtyard, [mischievously] and they let the Glessners pull off a trick. On 1 December 1887 the family moved everything in through here, [amused] 'before our neighbors suspected even that we were about to move'. [short pause] [warmly] That night they lit the new hearth with live fire carried from the old one.
scripts.stop:door: The front door: heavy oak strapped with iron, a square window behind an iron grille. Richardson would not have the ironwork painted; it was Bower-Barffed against rust, [curious] a process Glessner never saw anywhere else. [short pause] The wall looks like solid rock... but it is brick faced with granite slabs, with deep stones at every opening to keep up the illusion.
scripts.stop:porte: [playfully] Not every visitor uses the front door. Here a carriage could leave Prairie Avenue and roll right under the house, through two paneled oak doors hung on heavy iron straps, and out into a private courtyard. [short pause] Follow it through.
scripts.stop:court-north: [warmly] Inside, the house changes its mind. From the street it looked shut tight; here... it opens up. Richardson put generous windows on this sunny courtyard side, letting in, Glessner wrote, [amused] 'a flood of sunlight when the sun shines in Chicago'. [softly] The family rooms look in on this quiet yard, not out at the street.
scripts.stop:hall-bow: The rounded bay above the terrace steps is the entrance hall. Its door to this courtyard is glazed with yellow glass under chipped white glass, so the hall feels sunny even on grey days. [fondly] The vines here came from the family's old house; one was fifty-five feet long, and replanted whole. [short pause] It flourished.
scripts.stop:family: [warmly] Behind these walls, 1904 is a busy year. Frances Glessner, who has kept a journal since 1879, has set up a silversmith's bench in the basement. Every winter and spring her Monday Morning Reading Class meets in the library. [chuckles] Years ago her son George's friends ran a telegraph company from his school room... wired to seven houses.
scripts.ending:finish: [softly] Richardson never saw any of this. About three weeks before he died in April 1886, too ill to leave his bedroom, he marked on the drawings where the lights would go, and told Glessner: [quietly] 'There, Mr. Glessner... if I were to live five years longer, that is the last thing I would do on your house. My part is finished.' [long pause] Digging began that June, and George and Frances threw the first soil. [warmly] Glessner was convinced it was the house Richardson would most have liked to live in himself.
